findings.title: Token HTML-escaped but not URL-encoded before href substitution — latent URL-breakage risk
findings.description: In buildVerificationBody and buildPasswordResetBody, htmlEscape(token) is substituted into a URL query-string position inside an href attribute (e.g. href="{APP_URL}/auth/verify-email?token={TOKEN}"). HTML-escaping is the correct final encoding for text placed into an HTML attribute, but it does not URL-encode the token value first. Characters that are valid in a token but are not URL-safe (e.g. '+', '=', '#', '%', ' ') would be embedded verbatim in the query-string before HTML-escaping, producing a malformed URL that silently breaks the verification link. The current TokenService produces base64url tokens (alphabet [A-Za-z0-9_-], no padding), so the current callers are safe — but there is no assertion in EmailService that enforces this contract. A future change to standard base64 (which uses '+', '/' and '=') or a different token scheme would silently produce broken links without any test catching it.
findings.impact: If the token format ever shifts away from strict base64url, all verification and password-reset links would be silently malformed. Affected users would be unable to verify accounts or reset passwords. This is a silent operational failure with no error log, no metric, and no test catching it.

findings.title: No XSS regression test for token escaping — only name escaping is covered
findings.description: The single XSS test (sendVerificationEmail_htmlEscapesNameWithSpecialChars, line 57-62) passes a malicious name ('') but uses a clean token value ('token123'). There is no test that passes a malicious token value (e.g. '"onload=alert(1) x="' or '') and asserts that htmlEscape is applied to it in the resulting body. A refactoring that accidentally removes htmlEscape from the token substitution line would not be caught by the current test suite.
findings.impact: XSS regression risk: the htmlEscape fix for token (round 1, finding 1) has no test coverage. A future developer could revert the fix or introduce an analogous bug in a new template without any test failing.

findings.title: htmlEscape does not guard against null input — NullPointerException propagates synchronously
findings.description: The htmlEscape static method (line 106-113) calls input.replace(...) directly without a null check. If any caller passes null as name, token, or supportEmail, a NullPointerException is thrown inside buildVerificationBody / buildPasswordResetBody / buildAccountBlockedBody — synchronously, before sendAsync is called. This NPE propagates to the caller (e.g. AuthService) unhandled and uncaught by the Mono.fromCallable / subscribe error handler. In a reactive pipeline, a synchronous exception thrown outside a Mono may crash the subscribing thread rather than being handled as a Mono error signal, depending on the call site.
findings.impact: If a null name or token is ever passed (e.g. from a MongoDB document with a missing field, a test fixture, or a future code path), the service throws an unlogged, unhandled NPE. The email is silently not sent, the caller may receive an unexpected 500, and there is no log entry or metric about the failure.

findings.title: from address passed to MimeMessageHelper.setFrom() without validation — SMTP header injection risk
findings.description: The from field (injected from @Value("${app.mail.from}"), default 'noreply@botfunnel.local') is passed directly to MimeMessageHelper.setFrom(from) at line 82 without format validation or sanitization. A misconfigured or environment-variable-injected value containing CRLF characters (\r\n) could cause SMTP header injection, allowing an attacker with control over the MAIL_FROM environment variable to inject arbitrary mail headers (Bcc, Cc, Content-Type) into every outgoing email. While this requires compromising the deployment environment, it is a defense-in-depth gap consistent with the treatment applied to other config values.
findings.impact: If the MAIL_FROM environment variable is compromised or misconfigured with CRLF characters, an attacker could inject Bcc headers to silently copy all outgoing emails (verification, password reset, account-blocked) to an attacker-controlled address. This could expose tokens and PII to a third party.

findings.title: Hardcoded super-admin password in test properties committed to source control
findings.description: The file backend/src/test/resources/application-test.properties (line 4) contains SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD=test-admin-password. This value is committed to source control. While it is labelled a test fixture, it represents a hardcoded credential pattern that violates the project's own security rules (ALWAYS add secrets to .gitignore). If the same value is accidentally reused in a production deployment — or if a developer copies the test properties file as a starting point for a production config — the credential would be weak and already known. Additionally, secret scanning tools (e.g., gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning) may flag this and block CI/CD pipelines.
findings.impact: A hardcoded password in source control is a credential exposure risk. If the value is ever reused in production, an attacker with access to the repository (or its forks/CI logs) would already know the super-admin password, bypassing authentication entirely.
findings.recommendation:
Replace the hardcoded value with a randomly generated placeholder that cannot be mistaken for a real credential:

SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD=REPLACE_WITH_RANDOM_VALUE_IN_ENV

For local test runs that actually need a working super-admin, use a .env.test file (gitignored) or a Spring test @TestPropertySource that generates a random password per test run:

@Value("${SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD:#{T(java.util.UUID).randomUUID().toString()}}") String superAdminPassword

Also ensure application-test.properties is listed in .gitignore or that the CI pipeline populates the value from a GitHub Actions secret.
